The Czochralski method is the main industrial process for producing over 95% of high-quality (semiconductor grade) silicon single crystals and about 45% of lower-quality (solar grade) silicon crystals.
Crystals of SiC, AlN, and GaN cannot be grown from the melt at atmospheric pressure due to their thermal instability and decomposition at high temperatures.
The Grashof number (Gr) and the Reynolds number (Re) are key dimensionless numbers that characterize natural and forced convection, respectively, in crystal growth processes.
The Prandtl number (Pr) varies widely in crystal growth, from 0.01 for Si and Si-Ge melts to tens for oxide melts, which leads to qualitative differences in the convection patterns.

Modeling the turbulent flow in Czochralski growth of large-diameter silicon crystals (>300 mm) requires Reynolds numbers based on the crystal and crucible rotation speeds of the order of 10^5 and 3x10^5, respectively.

Direct numerical simulation (DNS) of turbulence in crystal growth setups is computationally prohibitive, requiring grid sizes on the order of 10^9-10^10 cells to resolve the wide range of length scales.
The Schmidt number (Sc) for oxygen in silicon melts is around 10, necessitating very fine computational grids to accurately model the oxygen transport.
Sublimation growth is used to produce SiC, AlN, and ZnO crystals, taking advantage of the congruent transfer of material from the solid source to the growing crystal.
Ammonothermal growth and the alkali metal method have been developed to grow III-nitride crystals at lower temperatures and pressures compared to the high-pressure solution growth approach.

Modeling of crystal growth processes requires the coupled solution of heat transfer by conduction, convection, and radiation, as well as mass transfer, electromagnetic effects, and crystal quality assessment.
